shadow:
There is a kind of need that hides itself by looking like love. It says I cannot manage without you, and it means it. The other person becomes the place you keep your footing. When they move, you fall.

A child reaches for the hand and the hand is there, and reaching becomes a habit before it ever becomes a question. So a grown person can spend years arranging life around someone who holds them up, and never once feel the floor under their own feet, because they have never had to stand on it alone.

Most people read this as devotion and leave it there. That is the misread. Need that big is not closeness. It is two people each holding the other up so neither finds out whether they can stand. The bond feels warm and it is also a cage, and the cage has a door, which is the part nobody mentions. The need is a signal pointing at the exact spot where your own ground has not been laid yet. You do not kill the need. You follow it down to the place it keeps pointing, and you start putting weight there, slowly, while it still scares you.
repressive: Some people meet this by clinging. They cannot let the old thing go, and they pull on the people near them with guilt, with small dramas, with the quiet ache of being unable to cope. It reads as love. It is fear of the empty room.
reactive: Others meet it by shutting the door. They announce they need no one, and they make sure everyone watches them say it. Underneath the proud solitude there is anger, and it spills the moment somebody actually comes close.
gift:
Something changes when a person stops leaning and learns to stand. Not coldly, not by walling anyone out. They simply get their feet under them, and from that footing a strange thing opens up. They start to feel everyone else.

This is sensitivity, and it is not the bruised, flinching kind. Real sensitivity is steady. It is the gift of touch, the skin reading the room before a word is spoken, the body knowing an animal is afraid or a friend is about to cry. You could only feel another person this clearly once you were no longer drowning in your own need of them.

There is an art to it the old name caught well. Approach. The sensitive one does not lunge. They wait at the edge of a thing and let it come to them at its own pace, the way you let a wary dog decide. They talk less and listen more. Because they can feel where a relationship has gone lopsided, they name it gently, before it festers. The cost is that they feel the world's grief too, which is heavy, and they carry it anyway, leaning a little further in instead of away.
siddhi:
Far enough along, the leaning stops being a problem to solve and becomes a thing freely given. This is sacrifice, and not the small kind, the kind where a person bleeds themselves dry for others and calls it virtue. That is just the old need wearing a halo.

The true thing happens inside. A person lets go of the separate self the way you finally set down a bag you forgot you were carrying. Not loss. Relief. The one who needed to be held, and then needed to prove they needed no one, is simply not standing there anymore.

What is left belongs to everything. It works for the whole without keeping score, without noticing it is working, because there is no longer a small self to feed first. The greatest of these lives go unseen, and that is fine, that is the point. Look back from here and the early clinging was not weakness. It was the first crude shape of a reach that always wanted to go this far, all the way out, holding nothing back.
